corrected_instrument_cite: Kappler II 594, Art. 5 (11 Stat. 749 is only an explanatory note, not the treaty text)
notes: Boundary text and the Art. 5 proviso (no abandonment of rights or claims to other lands; hunting, fishing and passage kept) match Kappler. ICC (4 Ind. Cl. Comm. 30-A, 1955) later held the treaty recognized aboriginal title; see local icc/d329_v04_p030a.txt.

source_title: Statutes at Large vol. 11, note "Treaty of Fort Laramie"
source_quote: certain amendments were made which require the assent of the Tribes, parties to it, before it can be considered a complete instrument. This assent of all the Tribes has not been obtained
corrected_summary: The Senate amended the 1851 treaty in 1852 (Kappler prints the amended annuity term: $50,000 a year for ten years, plus up to five more at the President's discretion). The amendments needed tribal assent, and the official Statutes note says the assent of all the tribes had not been obtained, so the treaty was never proclaimed or printed, though Congress appropriated money under it. Kappler's headnote calls it "never ratified or printed." Status: Senate-amended, never completed or proclaimed. Neither "ratified" nor "never ratified" alone is accurate.
notes: This overrides round-1 "contradicted": the federal record itself (11 Stat. 749 note; Kappler headnote "[The following treaty, though never ratified or printed, is sometimes referred to in appropriations") supports calling the status incomplete or contested. The NARA-catalog claim was not checked. The original 50-year term is not in the local text, which prints the amended version. Merged rows PSL-SCA-036 and PSL-CHY-B-035 take the same verdict.

notes: Art. 6 head-chief clause is confirmed. The claim that Arapaho governance had no head chief is Fowler 2015 (AIQ 39(4):367), not read here. Kappler prints no signature list, so the signers Little Owl, Big Man and Cut Nose were not verified. Settle with Fowler 2015 and the original treaty (NARA, unratified treaty file T494).

notes: Art. 3 protection duty is confirmed in the text. The Arapaho and Cheyenne understanding that the spoken council was the treaty is from Fowler 2015:366 and Roberts 1984:65-66 (not read). Settle with those sources or the council minutes (D. D. Mitchell report, ARCIA 1851).

notes: Art. 4 binds the tribes to restitution; Art. 8 lets the US withhold annuities; no article gives tribes a remedy against the US. Art. 3 does bind the US to protect against depredations, but provides no enforcement.

source_title: Kansas-Nebraska Act, May 30, 1854, sec. 19 (Kansas proviso)
source_quote: or to include any territory which, by treaty with any Indian tribe, is not, without the consent of said tribe, to be included within the territorial limits or jurisdiction of any State or Territory
corrected_summary: The Kansas-Nebraska Act did not exclude all Indian lands from Kansas Territory. It excluded only land that a treaty said could not be put in a territory without the tribe's consent, and it otherwise preserved Indian rights of person and property until extinguished by treaty. The 1851 Fort Laramie treaty has no such non-inclusion clause, so the Cheyenne-Arapaho land lay inside Kansas Territory's boundaries, but Indian title to it had not been extinguished. Creating Arapahoe County and opening it to settlement in 1855 ran against unextinguished Indian title and the 1834 Act, not against an exclusion from the territory.
notes: PSL's paraphrase "all Indian lands shall be excepted" (via Roberts 1984) overstates the proviso. The 1855 Kansas statute creating Arapahoe County was not checked.

source_title: Cofield v. McClelland (1873); Act of May 28, 1864 (Denver relief)
source_quote: was originally laid out by a company or association of persons, on the public domain of the United States, before the same had been
corrected_summary: Gold-rush town companies laid out Denver, Auraria and other towns in 1858-59, and Boulder in 1859, on land the 1851 treaty recognized as Cheyenne and Arapaho and that no treaty had yet ceded. The 1844 Townsite Act (5 Stat. 657) applied only to surveyed public lands, so it gave the town companies no title. Denver occupants got a path to title only through a special act of May 28, 1864 (13 Stat. 94), after Fort Wise; the probate judge entered the site on May 6, 1865. In 1873 the Supreme Court described the site as laid out "on the public domain" before survey: that is the federal view, written after the cessions. The 100,000 trespasser figure and the claim that no one was fined or removed under the 1834 Act were not verified.
corrected_instrument_cite: 4 Stat. 729 secs. 10-11 (1834 Act); 5 Stat. 657 (1844 Townsite Act); 13 Stat. 94 (1864 Denver act); 12 Stat. 1163 (Fort Wise)
notes: The 1864 act (local STAT-13-94.txt) extends the 1844 act to "authorize the probate judge of Arapahoe county, in the territory of" Colorado to enter secs. 33 and W1/2 34, T3S R68W. Cofield shows lot claims dating from 1859 (Preston) were litigated on possession at the 1865 entry, not on any 1858-59 town-company title. Black Hawk dating: the Gregory Gulch strike was 1859; the 1858 rush began with placer finds near Cherry Creek. This dating is general knowledge and was not checked against a primary source.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Wise, Feb. 18, 1861 (Statutes at Large)
source_quote: Little Raven, Storm, Shave-Head, and Big Mouth, (on the part of the Arapahoes,) and Black Kettle, White Antelope, Lean Bear, Little Wolf, Tall Bear, and Left Hand, or Namos, (on the part of the Cheyennes,)
corrected_summary: The treaty was made by commissioners A. G. Boone and F. B. Culver, not by Boone alone. The four Arapaho marks were Little Raven, Storm, Shave-Head and Big Mouth, all Southern. No Northern Arapaho signed. A "Left Hand, or Namos" signed on the Cheyenne side; he is a Cheyenne, not the Arapaho Left Hand (Niwot), who did not sign. The same ten men signed the assent to the Senate amendment on Oct. 29, 1861. The text says the signers were "duly authorized" by the confederated tribes; the claim that they said they spoke only for their own bands is from Roberts 1984 and Fowler 2015, not the treaty.
notes: Little Raven signed both in February and in October 1861, which bears on PSL's statement that he repudiated it. The hunger and no-negotiation claims are scholarly (Roberts, Fowler) and not in the primary text. Merged row WEB-DUR-024 takes the same verdict.

notes: The treaty text records no duress. The starvation threat is the descendants' account in exhibit text (ORAL_HISTORY), and PSL's own narrative says only that the Arapahos were hungry. Contemporaneous evidence is indirect: Evans (S. Rep. 156, App. 45-46) reports Fort Wise signers saying they had to repudiate it or the Dog Soldiers would kill them. Map label should read "Indigenous account: signed under threat of starvation", attributed to Cheyenne and Arapaho descendants. Settle with the Boone/Culver transmittal report (NARA RG 75, RIT 315).

Interpreter."), and the P.S. asks for 640 acres each for Robert Bent (Sulphur Spring, north side of the Arkansas, about five miles below the Pawnee Hills) and for Jack Smith, son of John S. notes: Boundary and the east-west split confirmed: the dividing line is 15 miles west of the Purgatoire, with the Arapaho share east of it ("the western boundary of that portion of said reservation to be hereafter occupied by the Arapahoes"). Non-delivery is supported by Delegate Bennet, Jan. 28, 1864 (ARCIA 1864 p. 245): "Three years have elapsed, and they are still wanderers from their lands". The 1863 Commissioner's report claimed the surveys were done and improvements under way. Colley's leasing to whites was not checked. Merged row PSL-FRD-014 takes the same verdict.

source_title: ICC findings of fact on value, Cheyenne-Arapaho, Dockets 329 and 348 (Dec. 6, 1961)
source_quote: officials of the Government were unsuccessful in securing a treaty of cession from them cntil the Treaty of May 10, 1868
corrected_summary: The federal record itself shows that Fort Wise did not settle the northern lands. Commissioner Dole's 1863 report says many bands were left out at Fort Wise and still claimed their right to the country had never been relinquished. Evans sought a further agreement in 1863 to get "an undoubted cession". The 1865 Little Arkansas treaty records the tribes' claim never to have relinquished title. The Indian Claims Commission found that only Southern bands were parties to Fort Wise and that the Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho ceded only by the treaty of May 10, 1868 (15 Stat. 655, Art. 2). Show the land north of the South Platte as not ceded by its occupants from 1861 to 1868. Browne's 1862-63 opinion was not seen and rests on Unrau 1964.
corrected_instrument_cite: 12 Stat. 1163 (Fort Wise); 15 Stat. 655 Art. 2 (1868 Northern cession); 10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1
notes: Supporting primaries: ARCIA 1863 p. 16 (Commissioner): "numbers of the bands were not included in the negotiations attending the treaty concluded with them at Fort Wise, whence arises the claim they so persistently urge" (local usindianaffairs63usdorich.txt); ARCIA 1863 p. 125 (Evans); 14 Stat. 703 Art. 2. The ICC also quotes agent W. W. Bent (1859) that the South Platte divided a northern band from a southern band. Royce 426's single 1861 cession date is wrong for the northern half.

source_title: Dole letter reversing Browne (1863)
source_cite: NARA RG 75, M234 (Colorado Superintendency) or Unrau 1964:310-311
notes: The Dole letter was not seen. The words "fait accompli" and "defiance of federal law" are Unrau's characterization. Indirect primary context: Dole's own 1863 report (ARCIA 1863 p. 16) admits the non-party bands claimed their right was never relinquished, and the ICC later found the northern cession happened only in 1868. Settle with the Dole letter (NARA M234) or Unrau 1964.

source_title: Upper Platte agreement of Aug. 19, 1863, with Loree certificate (ARCIA 1863)
source_quote: not to deliver their annuity goods to them until after the time appointed for the council with them
corrected_summary: On Aug. 19, 1863, at the Upper Platte agency, the Arapaho chiefs Black Bear, Roman Nose and Friday and the Cheyennes Spotted Horse and Shield made their marks on an agreement to abide by Fort Wise. Agent Loree certified he had told them his instructions were not to hand out annuity goods until after the council, and the paper states the annuities were distributed "in consideration of" the agreement. The withholding came from Loree's instructions for the treaty commission (Evans, Loree, Colley); the paper does not show a direct Evans order to withhold food. In July 1864 agent Whitely reported that Friday wanted a reserve on the north bank of the Cache la Poudre, from Box Elder Creek to the Platte and north to Crow Creek. That would have displaced about sixteen white families, and no reserve was made.
notes: Second source: ARCIA 1864 p. 235 (Whitely to Evans, July 14, 1864), local usindianaffairs64usdorich.txt. The OCR places the "Arapahoes" bracket by Black Bear, Roman Nose and Friday and "Cheyennes" by Spotted Horse and Shield; confirm the bracket placement on a page image.

source_title: Statement of Robert Bent, in Condition of the Indian Tribes (Doolittle report)
source_cite: S. Rep. No. 156, 39th Cong., 2d Sess. (1867), App. 96
source_quote: I have heard the Indians charge Major Colley with trading their own goods to them.
corrected_summary: Contemporaries accused agent Samuel G. Colley of diverting Arapaho and Cheyenne annuity goods. Robert Bent swore that goods being traded in the Sand Creek camp were "said to belong to Dexter Colley [the agent's son] and John Smith" and that Indians charged Colley with trading their own goods to them. Present this as a documented contemporaneous accusation, not a proven theft. That Colley was Dole's cousin rests on Unrau 1964:304 ("Dear Cousin William" letters), not checked here. The $3,000 from Evans was not verified.
notes: Same statement: "They were trading goods said to lielong to Dexter Col ley and John Smith." (OCR).

Rep. 156 App. 82) reprints the letter, it reads "make any peace" instead of "make any treaty". The JCCW report (1865, p. ii) says the chiefs "were led to believe that they were regarded in the light of friendly Indians." "Turned out to be a lie" is the characterization of PSL and Coel 1981.

source_quote: to the amount of five alternate sections per mile on each side of said railroad
corrected_summary: The 1862 Pacific Railway Act told the US to "extinguish as rapidly as may be the Indian titles" along the line, and it granted five alternate sections per mile on each side (ten sections, 6,400 acres, per mile), mineral lands excepted. "Ten square miles on each side" matches the 1864 amendment, which doubled the grant; that amendment was not checked here. That the two 1862 acts took homelands without tribal consent is the descendants' characterization (History Colorado exhibit). Evans's railroad grants were not verified.

notes: Docket 329-D is the Northern Arapaho docket, settled by compromise for $3,230,000 on June 27, 1963 (local icc/d329d_v12_p212.txt). The ICC valued the whole 51,210,000-acre tract at $23,500,000 as of Oct. 14, 1865, and held the Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho together owned a half interest (10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 64). source_title: Testimony of Gov. John Evans, Condition of the Indian Tribes (Doolittle report)
source_cite: S. Rep. No. 156, 39th Cong., 2d Sess. (1867), App. 45-46
source_quote: He said the white people had taken their gold and their lands
corrected_summary: Northern Arapaho leaders said in 1863 that whites had taken their gold and lands, and that they had not been at Fort Wise (Little Owl, reported by Evans). The ICC found that the Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho did not cede until the treaty of May 10, 1868. Gold mining from 1858 to 1868 therefore took place on land its northern occupants had not ceded. But the 1868 treaty (15 Stat. 655, Art. 2) relinquished all territory outside the reservations it named, and in 1963 the ICC paid the Northern Arapaho $3,230,000 in a compromise of the land claim (Docket 329-D). "Never signed a treaty and ceded" is accurate for 1858-1868 but not as a statement about the land today. Water rights were not checked.
notes: Evans also testified that the northern bands "took the ground that they bad [had] never sold their lands." This replaces round-1 "not_supported": the Northern position has contemporaneous federal documentation, but the claim of no cession at all is contradicted after 1868.

source_title: Indian Trade and Intercourse Act, June 30, 1834
source_quote: settlement on any lands belonging, secured, or granted by treaty with the
corrected_summary: The 1834 Act defined Indian country, "for the purposes of this act", as US land west of the Mississippi outside Missouri, Louisiana and Arkansas Territory. It fined anyone who settled on, or surveyed, land belonging to or secured by treaty to a tribe $1,000 (sec. 11). It authorized, but did not require, agents and the President to remove intruders, by military force if needed (secs. 10-11). It barred land purchases from Indians except by treaty (sec. 12). In 1834 the part of Colorado south of the Arkansas was Mexican territory; whether the Act covered it after 1848 depends on later extension acts, not checked here.
notes: "Shall have authority to remove" and "it shall, moreover, be lawful for the President" are permissive, so "required federal removal" overstates the Act. Merged row PSL-INT-012 takes the same verdict.

source_quote: This assent of all the Tribes has not been obtained
corrected_summary: The Senate amended the 1851 treaty, cutting the annuity term to ten years plus up to five at the President's discretion. The official Statutes note says the assent of all the tribes to the amendments was never obtained. The printed text says the nations themselves "selected" head chiefs (Art. 6). The claims that the US picked the signers, bypassed the Council of 44, and that amendment signatures did not match are TREC assertions without a cited source, not tested here.

source_title: ICC findings of fact, Cheyenne-Arapaho, Dockets 329 and 348 (Nov. 1, 1955)
source_quote: destroyed and depleted buffalo and game, the native grasses and forests, and threatened the livelihood
corrected_summary: The ICC found that emigrants and troops passing through before 1851 destroyed buffalo, game, grass and timber, causing hunger and loss of life. The treaty required the tribes to make restitution for their own people's wrongs (Art. 4) and had no article on restitution for game, timber or grass. But Art. 7 states the annuities were given partly "for the damages which have or may occur by reason thereof" to the nations, so the treaty did offer general compensation, though it did not single out those losses.
notes: Art. 7 text: "In consideration of the treaty stipulations, and for the damages which have or may occur by reason thereof to the Indian nations".

source_title: ICC findings of fact on value, Dockets 329 and 348
source_quote: officials of the Government were unsuccessful in securing a treaty of cession from them cntil the Treaty of May 10, 1868
corrected_summary: The Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho did not sign the 1861 Fort Wise treaty, and the ICC found they ceded only in 1868. Some northern chiefs did sign an annuity-conditioned agreement on Aug. 19, 1863, to abide by Fort Wise, which Evans himself called "not in proper treaty form" (ARCIA 1863 pp. 125, 131). Evans testified that Fort Wise signers told the trader Gerry they had to repudiate the treaty or the Dog Soldiers would kill them, and that the northern bands said they had never sold their lands (S. Rep. 156, App. 45-46). Left Hand's statement and Council of 44 non-approval were not checked.
notes: Evans quote, S. Rep. 156 App. 46: "the chiefs who signed that treaty told Gerry that they were obliged to repudiato the signing of that treaty of Fort -Wise, or the Dog soldiers would kill them." Merged row WEB-DUR-025 takes the same verdict.

source_title: Treaty of Fort Wise, Art. 6; Upper Platte agreement Aug. 19, 1863
source_quote: ratification of this treaty, shall not be entitled to the benefit of any of its stipulations
corrected_summary: Article 6 sets no required number of signers. It says bands that did not rejoin within one year of ratification lose the treaty's benefits. Marks were collected after 1861: on Aug. 19, 1863, Black Bear, Roman Nose, Friday, Spotted Horse and Shield signed an agreement to abide by Fort Wise, in exchange for release of their annuities, and that agreement was never submitted to the Senate. The accurate point is that the non-party bands never assented by any treaty before 1865 (Southern) or 1868 (Northern).
notes: Evans (ARCIA 1863 p. 125): "This contract, though not in proper treaty form, secures in effect an assent of these bands to the treaty of Fort Wise". The one-year deadline was tied to ratification, which the Senate gave Aug. 6, 1861, with proclamation Dec. 5, 1861.

source_title: Treaty with Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, May 10, 1868, Art. 2
source_quote: hereby relinquish, release, and surrender to the United States all right, claim, and interest in and to all territory outside the two reservations above mentioned
corrected_summary: No court ruling was found, and Browne's and Dole's 1862-63 views were not seen (Roberts 1984). Dole was Commissioner of Indian Affairs, not Interior Secretary. The narrower point has strong federal support: Fort Wise did not cede the lands of the non-party northern bands, and the ICC found they ceded only in 1868. But "still unceded today" is contradicted: the Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho relinquished all territory outside their reservations in 1868 (15 Stat. 655, Art. 2), the Southern tribes relinquished their claim to the whole Platte-Arkansas country in 1865 (14 Stat. 703, Art. 2), and the ICC paid compensation in 1963-65.
notes: Whatever the fairness of those instruments, the map should not label the area legally unceded today.

source_quote: John W. Wright, esquire, has been appointed a special agent to pur-
corrected_summary: John W. Wright was appointed in August 1863 as a special agent to buy goods for the Caddo refugees, with $4,000 put in his hands. The Commissioner's 1863 report says the Fort Wise reserve surveys "have been completed". Wright's lack of survey credentials, the faulty survey, Usher's friendship and the unusable houses rest on Kelsey 1968 and were not checked.
notes: The quote breaks across a hyphen in the OCR; the full phrase is "appointed a special agent to purchase certain articles for the Oaddo Indians". The $4,000 was for purchases, not salary.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 (citing Roberts 1984:143-144)
source_quote: This proposal’s aim was to extinguish land claims of the Utes, Comanche, Kiowa, and Plains Apache.
notes: Needs Evans's 1862 message to the Colorado territorial legislature (Colorado House/Council Journals 1862).

source_title: Pacific Railway Act, July 1, 1862
source_quote: railroad to the extent of two hundred feet in width on each side of said railroad where it may pass over the public lands
corrected_summary: The 1862 Act granted a right of way 200 feet wide on each side of the track (400 feet in all), directed the US to extinguish Indian title along the line, and granted five alternate sections per mile on each side (ten sections, 6,400 acres, per mile), mineral lands excepted. Evans's November 1863 New York meeting and the tie to his South Platte stance rest on Roberts and were not checked.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 (citing Roberts 1984:142)
source_quote: They had been fabricated by settlers who hoped their stories would lead to the removal of Indians from land which the settlers had stolen.
notes: Needs the July 1862 military and agent reports (ARCIA 1862, Official Records). "Fabricated by settlers" is Roberts's and TREC's characterization.

source_title: Upper Platte agreement, Aug. 19, 1863 (ARCIA 1863)
source_quote: and in consideration of the above agreement, we have our annuities distributed to us.
corrected_summary: On Aug. 19, 1863, the Arapahoes Black Bear, Roman Nose and Friday and the Cheyennes Spotted Horse and Shield signed an agreement at the Upper Platte agency to abide by Fort Wise. The document itself says annuities were distributed in consideration of the agreement, and Loree certified he had been instructed not to deliver goods until after the council. The paper does not say "no gifts were given"; it says the opposite. The threats by other chiefs against Spotted Horse and Shield were not found in this source.
corrected_instrument_cite: Agreement of Aug. 19, 1863, ARCIA 1863 pp. 131-132 (not a ratified instrument)
notes: Round-1 "confirmed" was too strong on the gift point. "Roman Nose" here is listed with the Arapahoes in the OCR bracket; check the page image.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 (citing Grinnell 1915; Trenholm 1970; Hoig 1961)
source_quote: starvation “would probably be the easier way of disposing of them.”
notes: The Anthony quote was not found in the local JCCW 1865 report or S. Rep. 156. Hunger on the reserve is confirmed in general by Bennet, Jan. 28, 1864 (ARCIA 1864 p. 245): "already the red man finds hunger and starvation staring him". Settle with Anthony's letter as quoted in Grinnell 1915:125-128.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 (citing Roberts 1984; Trenholm 1970)
source_quote: It may have been that Left Hand was not wanted in the delegation because he spoke fluent English, and trickery would have been made more difficult with him there.
notes: The motive is TREC's inference, flagged by TREC itself. The 1863 Washington delegation is mentioned in ARCIA 1863, but Left Hand's exclusion was not checked.

source_title: Whitely to Evans, July 14, 1864 (ARCIA 1864)
source_quote: the driving off of some sixteen families of whites who have made valuable improvements
corrected_summary: In 1864 agent Simeon Whitely reported that the Arapaho chief Friday "insists very strongly" on a reserve on the north bank of the Cache la Poudre, from Box Elder Creek to the Platte and north to Crow Creek. Whitely objected that it would mean driving off about sixteen white families, would cross the Overland stage route, and lay far from timber. No reserve resulted. The phrase "in exchange for peace", Whitely's incompetence and his hotel stay rest on Kelsey 1968.
notes: The talks were in mid-1864 (letters of July 3-14, 1864), not early 1864.

source_title: Bennet to Dole, Jan. 28, 1864 (ARCIA 1864, doc. No. 96)
source_quote: therefore they ask that the troops stationed at Fort Lyon, C. T., may be removed from their reservation
notes: Bennet writes that a War Department military reservation took the very lands the Arapahoes wished to farm, that "Three years have elapsed, and they are still wanderers from their lands", and that if Fort Lyon were evacuated the Arapahoes would occupy their lands. That last point is Bennet's expectation, not a recorded promise by the chiefs. Dole (Feb. 2, 1864, No. 97) declined to recommend removal.

source_title: H. T. Ketchum to Evans, Fort Larned, April 4, 1864 (ARCIA 1864, doc. No. 113)
source_quote: Spotted Wolf says those of his band alone have traded two hundred robes this season for whiskey.
corrected_summary: Special agent Ketchum reported in April 1864 that the six tribes near Fort Larned did "not realize one-fourth" of robe value from traders, and that Spotted Wolf's band alone had traded 200 robes for whiskey. He wrote of the tribes generally, not of the Cheyenne only. Watered whiskey worth $0.25 and trader Beggs's bills were not seen in the part of the report read.
notes: Ketchum also reports the sutler at Fort Lyon selling whiskey to Little Raven and Left Hand.

source_title: Testimony of Jacob Downing, Condition of the Indian Tribes
source_quote: I captured an Indian and required him to go to the village, or I would kill him.
corrected_summary: Maj. Jacob Downing testified that in mid-May 1864 he forced a captured Indian to guide him "or I would kill him", surprised a Cheyenne village at Cedar Bluffs about sixty miles north of the South Platte, killed (as he was told) about 26 and wounded 30, burned the lodges, took no prisoners, and gave the captured stock to his men. The pyre threat and the identification of the captive as Spotted Horse are not in Downing's testimony. The campaign followed a dispute over the rancher Ripley's stock, not a single stolen horse.
notes: This is the Cedar Canyon (Cedar Bluffs) fight, May 1864, as the round-1 note guessed.

source_title: Evans to Colley, Sept. 29, 1864; JCCW report 1865
source_cite: ARCIA 1864 p. 220; JCCW (1865) Massacre of Cheyenne Indians pp. ii-iii
source_quote: I have declined to make any treaty with them lest it might embarrass the military operations
corrected_summary: After Camp Weld, Evans declined to make a treaty "lest it might embarrass the military operations." The JCCW found that the chiefs' bands went to Fort Lyon on Evans's and Chivington's suggestion, were "treated somewhat as prisoners of war", gave up their arms, and were then told rations would stop. Anthony sent them to Sand Creek. Chivington attacked on Nov. 29 while Black Kettle flew a US flag with a white flag under it. Chivington's words "They won't be prisoners after we get there" and the claim that his Nov. 24 report was fabricated were not found in the sources read.
notes: JCCW quote: "They were called together and told that rations could no longer be issued to them". The $30 million figure and Soule's murder were not checked.

source_title: JCCW, Massacre of Cheyenne Indians (1865), report
source_quote: to remove from office those who have thus disgraced the government by whom they are employed
corrected_summary: The Joint Committee condemned Evans's testimony for "prevarication and shuffling", quoted his Aug. 11, 1864 proclamation inviting citizens to kill hostile Indians and keep their property, and urged that those responsible be removed from office and punished. The report text does not name Evans in a call for resignation. Bradford's charges and Seward's July 18, 1865 request were not checked.
notes: Evans's Aug. 11, 1864 proclamation is printed in ARCIA 1864 pp. 230-231: citizens may "hold to their own private use and benefit, all the property of said hostile Indians that they may capture".

source_title: Treaty of the Little Arkansas with Cheyenne and Arapaho, Oct. 14, 1865
source_cite: 14 Stat. 703, Arts. II, III, V, VI, VII and Senate amendment 1
source_quote: a reservation, no part of which shall be within the State of Kansas
corrected_summary: The treaty was ratified with amendments (May 22, 1866), the amendments were accepted (Nov. 10 and 19, 1866), and it was proclaimed Feb. 2, 1867, so "never ratified" is wrong. The promised reservation was never set up, because the Senate amendment required a reserve outside Kansas, with tribal assent, and none was designated before Medicine Lodge (1867). Art. II itself made settlement wait until the US extinguished other tribes' title. Art. VI granted 320 acres to each of four named chiefs and 160 acres to each widow or orphan of Sand Creek. Art. V granted 640 acres to named mixed-blood relatives. Art. VII paid $20 per capita before removal and $40 after.
corrected_royce_areas: 426 (cession of claim, Art. II); 477 (Fort Wise reserve)
notes: Art. II also records the 1851 territory as "country they claim to have originally owned, and never to have" relinquished. Attendance (one sixth of the Cheyenne) and the Dog Soldiers' refusal were not checked.

source_title: Treaty of the Little Arkansas, Art. VI
source_quote: grant three hundred any twenty acres of land by patent to each of the following-named chiefs
notes: The Art. VI reparations promise is confirmed. The bills of 1949, 1957 and 1965 and Flute v. United States (D. Colo. 2013; 10th Cir. 2015; cert. denied 2016) were not checked; settle with the 10th Circuit opinion. The round-1 note says the dismissal was on sovereign immunity grounds.

source_title: Treaty of the Little Arkansas with Comanche and Kiowa, Oct. 18, 1865
source_quote: an amount which shall be equal to fifteen dollars per capita
corrected_summary: The Kiowa-Comanche reserve (Art. II) ran from the northeast corner of New Mexico south and east to the Red River, the 98th meridian and the Cimarron, so it covered the Texas Panhandle as well as western Indian Territory. Annuities were $10 per capita before removal and $15 after. Art. III allowed them to range south of the Arkansas, and written permission from the agent was needed to leave the reserve. Dole's instruction about abandoning the Platte valley rests on Waltmann 1962 and was not checked.
notes: Ratified May 22, 1866; proclaimed May 26, 1866.

source_title: Report of the Indian Peace Commissioners, Jan. 7, 1868
source_cite: H.R. Ex. Doc. No. 97, 40th Cong., 2d Sess. (1868), p. 12
source_quote: he at once ordered the Indian village, of about three hundred lodges together with the entire property of the tribes, to be burned.
corrected_summary: In April 1867 Hancock marched on a Cheyenne-Lakota village on the Pawnee Fork despite the chiefs' pleas; the women and children fled "having the remembrance of Sand creek." After word came that the fleeing Indians had killed men at a Smoky Hill station, Hancock ordered the village burned. The Peace Commission put it at about 300 lodges, not the 110 Cheyenne and 140 Sioux lodges TREC gives. Stanley's $100,000 estimate was not checked. Kansas, not Colorado.
notes: Royce: no Colorado area.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 (citing RIT 364 documents)
source_quote: considered them all of inferior quality, “more so that [sic] any goods I ever saw delivered to the Indians.”
notes: Needs NARA Ratified Treaty file 364 or ARCIA 1868.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 (citing RIT 364; Roberts 2016; Campbell 2022)
source_quote: Big Head, who described himself as half chief and half Dog Soldier, said he would not sign anything unless the children who had been taken at Sand Creek were returned.
notes: The figure of 30 children is a single personal communication. Needs the Indian Peace Commission proceedings (October 1867) for Big Head's statement and Sanborn's motion.

source_title: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek (Cheyenne and Arapaho), Oct. 28, 1867, Art. XI
source_quote: on any lands south of the Arkansas so long as the buffalo may range
corrected_summary: The written treaty reserves hunting only "on any lands south of the Arkansas", with no hunting right between the Arkansas and South Platte. The claim that Henderson promised such a right orally rests on Jones 1966 and Gard 1959 and was not checked here.
notes: The absence from the text is confirmed; the oral promise is scholarly.

source_title: Treaty with the Cherokee, July 19, 1866, Art. XVI; Medicine Lodge Art. II
source_cite: 14 Stat. 799, Art. XVI; 15 Stat. 593, Art. II
source_quote: The United States may settle friendly Indians in any
corrected_summary: The 1867 Medicine Lodge reserve lay between Kansas's south line (37th parallel) and the Cimarron, inside the Cherokee Outlet. The Cherokee still held that land, but their 1866 treaty (Art. XVI) let the US settle friendly tribes west of 96 degrees, with payment to the Cherokee. So the US had a treaty right to place tribes there, though not title. The Cheyenne-Arapaho reserve was later fixed by the executive order of Aug. 10, 1869. Water quality and Hazen's declaration were not checked.
notes: Kappler I (1891 Cherokee agreement) refers to the "Cheyenne and Arapahoe Reservation, created or defined by Executive order dated August 10, 1869."

source_title: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek, Senate resolution of July 25, 1868
source_quote: Senate advise and consent to the ratification of the treaty between the United States and the Cheyenne and Arapaho[e] tribes of Indians
corrected_summary: The Senate consented to the Cheyenne-Arapaho Medicine Lodge treaty on July 25, 1868, without any amendment, and it was proclaimed Aug. 19, 1868. Brill's claim that the Senate struck an article on back annuities and Little Arkansas restitution is not borne out by the official ratification record. Any such article would have to have been dropped before signing.
notes: TREC itself flagged that only Brill makes this claim.

source_title: Treaty of Medicine Lodge Creek, Art. VIII
source_quote: not exceeding in value one hundred dollars
notes: Art. VIII: up to $100 in seeds and implements the first year, and up to $25 for each of three further years. The mule, wagon and oxen prices were not checked. The "open-air prison" quote is NPS commentary, not about this article.

source_title: Treaty with Northern Cheyenne and Northern Arapaho, May 10, 1868
source_quote: TAH-ME-LA-PASH-ME, or Dull Knife.
notes: Thirteen Indian marks are printed (Black Bear, Medicine Man, Little Wolf, Short Hair, Sorrel Horse, The Under Man, The Man in the Sky, The Big Wolf, The Beau, The Man that falls from his horse, White Crow, Little Shield, Dull Knife), none labeled by tribe or band. "Not representative" is TREC's characterization. The Crow treaty is a separate instrument.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 (citing Dodge 1877; Smits 1994; Feir et al. 2022)
source_quote: On the advice of Secretary Delano, Grant pocket vetoed this legislation after it finally made its way through Congress.
notes: The 1874 pocket veto can be settled with the Congressional Record (43rd Cong., 1st Sess., H.R. 921). The other figures are secondary.

source_title: PSL TREC 2024 (citing Calloway 2013; Prucha 1994; ARCIA 1868)
source_quote: the treaty process was “a fraud from beginning to end, manipulated, directed, and controlled by Indian agents and superintendents
notes: This is TREC's interpretive fraud theory; the Clarke quote comes via Prucha 1994. Primary checks elsewhere in this batch support parts of it: annuities used to get assent (1863 agreement), oral terms left out (Medicine Lodge Art. XI), and non-party bands bypassed (Dole 1863). The appropriation status as of March 3, 1869 (ARCIA 1868 p. 6) was not checked.

source_title: ICC, Cheyenne-Arapaho, opinion and findings on value (1961); compromise findings (1965)
source_cite: 10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 64 (1961); 16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162 (1965), Dockets 329-A, 329-B
source_quote: half interest in subject tract of 51,210,000 acres which had a fair market value as of October 14, 1865, of $23,500,000.00
corrected_instrument_cite: ICC Dockets 329, 329-A, 329-B: value 10 Ind. Cl. Comm. 1 (1961); compromise 16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162 (1965)
notes: $23.5M / 51.21M acres = $0.459 an acre. The Southern tribes settled Dockets 329-A and 329-B for $15,000,000 "in settlement of all claims" (16 Ind. Cl. Comm. 162), so the $15M is a global settlement, not the land price. The Northern Arapaho settled Docket 329-D for $3,230,000 (1963) and the Northern Cheyenne 329-C for $4,360,886.19 (1963), per the ICC Final Report. The ICC dated the taking to Oct. 14, 1865, not to Fort Wise in 1861. The Holbrook and Hoyt appraisal figures were not found in the local OCR.
